terms.definition: A person with sufficient control over premises to owe a duty of care to those who come onto them.
terms.examiner: Wheat v Lacon: there can be more than one occupier.

terms.definition: The Act setting out the duty owed by an occupier to lawful visitors: the common duty of care.
terms.examiner: s2(2): to take reasonable care to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which they are invited.

terms.definition: A person with express or implied permission to be on the premises, including those entering by contract or legal right.
terms.examiner: A visitor who goes beyond their permission becomes a trespasser.

terms.definition: An occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults.
terms.examiner: Glasgow Corporation v Taylor (allurements); Phipps v Rochester (parents expected to supervise very young children).

terms.definition: The Act setting out the duty owed to people other than visitors, chiefly trespassers.
terms.examiner: s1(3): the duty arises only if the occupier knows of the danger, knows the trespasser may come into its vicinity and could reasonably be expected to offer protection. Tomlinson v Congleton.

terms.definition: An occupier is not liable for a contractor's faulty work if they took reasonable care to choose a competent contractor and, where possible, checked the work.
terms.examiner: Haseldine v Daw; Woodward v Mayor of Hastings.
